articles.headline: Economy Grows 3.4% While Prices Climb 3.6%, Giving Fed Two Reasons to Keep Watching
articles.dek: Third-quarter GDP beat forecasts as September inflation accelerated, a day after the Fed held rates at 3.75%-4% and promised to evaluate incoming data.
articles.catch_up: The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate steady, saying it could afford to wait for more information. On Thursday, the Commerce Department delivered a large amount of it.
articles.why_it_matters: Strong growth and sticky inflation make rate cuts harder to justify, which keeps borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans and business debt elevated. The data also suggests energy prices, not just AI spending, are shaping what households pay.
body: The U.S. economy grew at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, beating the 3.1% economists expected and the 2.2% recorded in the second quarter, the Commerce Department reported Thursday, according to CNBC. In the same release cycle, the department said inflation picked up in September. The economy, in other words, is doing more of everything, including getting more expensive.
Translation: an annualized rate means the quarter's growth is projected as if it lasted a full year. It is a way of making a three-month period sound more decisive than it was.

The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index, rose 0.5% in September, the largest monthly gain since March. That put the annual rate at 3.6%, a tenth of a point below forecasts. Excluding food and energy, the core reading was 0.3% for the month and 3.1% for the year, matching expectations. Officials generally treat core as the better guide to longer-term trends, since they cannot do much about the price of gasoline, a fact they tend to mention only when asked.
The Fed's target is 2%. The 3.6% headline figure is therefore a target in the way a restaurant's posted closing time is a target.

The September jump was driven by energy. Gasoline and other energy goods rose 9.2% for the month, and energy goods and services broadly rose 5.4%. Economists fear this could spread elsewhere, CNBC reported. Services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4% and housing costs rose 0.3%, which suggests the spreading may already have begun in a modest, unhurried way. Brent crude stood at 123.1 in the latest official data, which gives the worry some context.

There was a better number buried in the quarterly view. PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline measure and 2.5% on core, down from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. So inflation over the quarter looked calm, while the final month looked less so. Both statements are true, which is the central difficulty of reading economic data.

Growth came from the usual suspects. Consumer spending rose 3.8%, the same as the prior quarter. Private domestic investment soared 19.4%, with equipment spending up 20.9% and intellectual property products up 8.4%, reflecting the artificial intelligence build-out. Real sales to private domestic purchasers, which Fed officials use as a proxy for underlying demand, rose 4.9%.

In September itself, consumer spending rose 0.5% against a forecast of 0.6%, and personal income rose 0.2% against a forecast of 0.3%. Households are spending slightly faster than they are earning, a pattern that can continue until it cannot. Meanwhile, initial jobless claims fell to 194,000, below the 200,000 forecast and near levels last seen in the late 1960s.

The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, held its rate at 3.75%-4% on Wednesday. Warsh said the period ahead is "information rich." Thursday's data added to the pile and suggested, in CNBC's words, that the Fed could have more work to do. Chris Rupkey of Fwdbonds said growth is powering ahead despite geopolitical risks and the damage higher energy costs inflict on many sectors.

Markets took it with restraint. Stock futures slipped and Treasury yields fell. The latest official data put the 10-year yield at 5.05% and the 2-year at 4.67%, so the bond market continues to charge a premium for patience. The Fed has said it will keep reading. There is now a great deal to read.
articles.wire_headline: Third-quarter U.S. GDP increases a better-than-expected 3.4% as September inflation accelerates

articles.headline: Fed Holds Rates, Skips Future Votes, Rearranges Reporters Alphabetically in Reverse
articles.dek: The Federal Open Market Committee held its rate at 3.75% to 4% on a 10-2 vote, with two dissenters wanting a hike, while Chairman Kevin Warsh announced the Fed will vote on rates less often.
articles.catch_up: The Fed raised rates in September under new Chairman Kevin Warsh after holding them in June and July, while inflation stayed well above its 2% target. Markets spent October guessing whether another hike would arrive this week.
articles.why_it_matters: A Fed that votes less often and signals less clearly makes borrowing costs harder to predict for mortgage holders, businesses and investors. Two dissenters and several economists are betting the next move is up, with inflation at 3.74% by the latest reading.
body: The Federal Reserve voted 10-2 on Wednesday to hold its benchmark rate at a range of 3.75% to 4%. According to the Fed's statement, the committee called economic activity strong, inflation elevated, and promised to deliver price stability. It did not say when.

The two dissents are the real story of the vote. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both preferred a quarter-point increase. CNBC reported that Cook had never dissented on a rate vote since taking her seat in 2022, and that governors rarely do. Translation: when the people who normally agree start disagreeing, the room is paying attention.

Chairman Kevin Warsh then held a news conference that CNBC's analysis described as a break from his early, cornered-looking appearances. He said that if the Fed had a firm conclusion about policy, it would announce it with much fanfare. He also said that while financial conditions are tighter, he is unwilling and unable to call them tight. Translation: the Fed has not decided to hike, and has not decided not to, and would like you to read the sentence carefully.

The deliberate vagueness has a history. Warsh was appointed by a president who called rate cuts a litmus test for the job, according to CNBC. After holds in June and July, commentators questioned his credibility. The September hike answered them, and then markets swung so far toward another hike that two top officials appeared to talk expectations back down. Warsh declined to confirm he had directed them. Fed insiders say vice chairs usually coordinate messaging with the chair, so the denial offers what CNBC called plausible deniability.

The bigger change is procedural. The Fed will still meet eight times in 2027, but one meeting will have no rate vote and no statement. In 2028 two meetings will be so designated. Translation: the Fed is keeping the meetings and removing the part where anything happens. That leaves six scheduled chances to move rates in 2027, plus emergency meetings, which the chairman can call at any time. CNBC's analysis noted this devalues Fedspeak, since a regional president's remarks matter less when a decision is months away, and those presidents lose a scheduled vote in their rotation.

Critics see a cost. Advocates of transparency argue that sunlight forces officials to sharpen their arguments. Robert Sockin of PGIM called holding a policy mistake and said a gradual Fed likely has to hike higher later, raising recession risk. Seema Shah of Principal Asset Management expects hikes in December and early 2027, while Jefferies' Thomas Simons declined to call Warsh either dovish or hawkish.

The press room has also been reorganized. Press conferences now run about half an hour, reporters get one question rather than two, and seating moved from loosely by outlet size to alphabetical in September, then reverse alphabetical this month. CNBC noted this keeps microphone bearers on their toes. It is the one Fed policy whose direction is perfectly clear.

The data will decide the next chapter. The 2-year Treasury yield sat at 4.67% and the 10-year at 5.05% as of Wednesday, both above the Fed's own policy rate of 3.88%. Markets are effectively saying they expect higher rates to come. The committee next meets in December, with a stack of new data in hand and, for now, a vote still scheduled.
articles.wire_headline: Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement

articles.headline: ECB Holds Rates, Announces Departure of President, Declines to Hold Either Quietly
articles.dek: The central bank kept its key rate at 2.5% as euro zone inflation hit 3.8%, while Christine Lagarde said she will leave in February to speak more freely.
articles.catch_up: The European Central Bank raised rates in June and September as energy prices jumped after the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February. On Thursday it paused, and its president announced she is leaving early.
articles.why_it_matters: The ECB's rate path sets borrowing costs for mortgages and businesses across 21 countries, and markets still see a decent chance of another hike in December. Who succeeds Lagarde could matter for how the bank handles France's rising bond yields.
body: The European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday, as markets expected, even though euro zone inflation reached 3.8% last month, the highest since September 2023, according to CNBC. Energy price inflation ran at 18.8%. The bank chose to do nothing about this, which in central banking is classed as a decision.

The reasoning, as President Christine Lagarde explained it, is that underlying inflation and wages have been broadly stable. Translation: second-round effects, meaning higher energy costs leaking into wages and prices everywhere else, have not yet shown up. She said the Governing Council debated a hike but unanimously settled on a pause, citing rising uncertainty and a "measured approach." A unanimous vote after a debate about doing the opposite is the central banker's version of a group photo.

Markets were unconvinced that the pause means peace. Money markets priced about a 67% chance of a hike in December, according to LSEG data. Deutsche Bank's Mark Wall expects one more hike to 2.75%, and UBS's Dean Turner called Thursday a "hawkish pause" rather than the end of tightening. Translation: the bank is stopping to catch its breath, not to put on its shoes for the day off.

Lagarde also noted that long-term borrowing costs are climbing globally, with the average 10-year sovereign yield up about 35 basis points since the last meeting (Translation: 0.35 percentage points). She attributed this partly to expectations for inflation and rates and partly to "debt issuance by some of the hyperscalers," who are issuing more long-term bonds and competing for the same lenders. Governments, it turns out, now share the bond market with companies building data centers.

Then came the second announcement. Lagarde will step down on Feb. 7, nearly nine months before her term ends in October 2027. She said she wants freedom of speech and expression on matters that are not monetary policy, because as president she was bound by an obligation of neutrality, which she called the price of independence. Her exit lands before France's presidential election, where polling suggests Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner. Aberdeen Investments' Felix Feather noted the new French president will have no role in choosing the next ECB head.

The succession is political despite the bank's formal independence. Appointments are made by the European Council after consulting the European Parliament and euro area states, with national balance in play. CNBC reports that Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot are widely seen as top contenders. Knot is seen as more hawkish, which analysts said could support the euro but add pressure to French and peripheral bond spreads. De Cos would signal continuity, according to Validus Risk Management.

The backdrop is France, where yields have spiked and the spread over German bonds is at its highest since the early 2010s debt crisis. Berenberg's Holger Schmieding said the ECB has "no mandate and no appetite to fund French fiscal follies" and would help only if Paris returns to sustainable policies. Eurostat data released Friday showed France's economy shrinking 0.1% in the third quarter, while the euro zone grew 0.4%, beating a forecast of 0.2%.

Lagarde, who got a standing ovation from the Governing Council, is reportedly a top candidate to chair the World Economic Forum, according to the Financial Times. That would let her speak freely, in a setting where speaking freely has historically been the main activity. Next to watch is the December meeting, where the bank will either hike or explain why it did not.
articles.wire_headline: European Central Bank keeps key interest rate on hold at 2.5%

articles.headline: Exxon and Chevron Hit Record Highs After Discovering That Fuel Shortages Are Profitable
articles.dek: The two oil giants posted combined third-quarter profits of $25.3 billion as refineries ran flat out and diesel reached $6.32 a gallon.
articles.catch_up: Since March, when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, attacks by Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants on refineries in Russia and the Middle East have cut global refining capacity by millions of barrels a day. Importers have turned to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries for diesel.
articles.why_it_matters: Diesel moves freight, farm equipment and construction, so a 70% jump in its price filters into the cost of nearly everything else. Meanwhile the companies selling it are posting record share prices.
body: Chevron and ExxonMobil reported sharply higher third-quarter profits on Friday, and both stocks touched all-time highs, according to CNBC. Exxon's profit doubled to $15.4 billion, while Chevron's net income rose nearly 200% to $9.9 billion. Both beat Wall Street expectations, which is the traditional way a company confirms that other people's problems are going well.

The mechanism is simple. Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants have attacked refineries in Russia and the Middle East, removing millions of barrels per day of capacity. Importers therefore need diesel from somewhere else, and the somewhere else is the U.S. Gulf Coast. Exxon's refineries there ran at 100% capacity utilization. Chevron's U.S. refineries ran at 98% and processed just over 1 million barrels a day, a record.

Translation: when a product is scarce and everyone must buy it anyway, the people who still have a working factory get to name the price. Exxon CEO Darren Woods put it more formally, telling CNBC that diesel is the crunch point because it is critical to growth, with "very inelastic demand." Translation: customers will keep paying whatever it costs, because trucks do not run on good intentions.

The refining divisions did most of the work. Chevron's refining profit rose more than 300% to $4.9 billion. Exxon's refining earned about $7.2 billion in the quarter, edging out its production business at about $7.1 billion. Exxon's refining profit for the first nine months reached $11.4 billion, against $4 billion a year earlier.

Pumping oil, by contrast, was not the story. Chevron's production slipped to 3.9 million barrels a day from about 4 million, partly because of the Middle East conflict. Exxon's output this year is down more than 2%. The companies are producing slightly less and earning far more, which is a business model economists usually call a market, and everyone else calls a bill.

That bill is visible at the pump. AAA put the U.S. national average for diesel at $6.32 a gallon on Friday, up more than 70% from a year earlier, after a record high in September. Brent crude stood at $123.10 in the latest data, and inflation was running at 3.74% as of September, so the fuel costs are not confined to truck stops.

The politics are awkward. CNBC noted that President Donald Trump said in August that the two companies "were making too much money based on a shortage." The companies appear to have taken this as a forecast rather than a criticism. Chevron CEO Mike Wirth, for his part, told CNBC that "the system is under stress" and that the environment is "fairly fragile."

Fragile is a useful word here. Record profits depend on refineries elsewhere staying broken and Gulf Coast plants staying at full tilt. Watch whether the shortage eases, and whether Washington's displeasure ever turns into something other than a remark.
articles.wire_headline: Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs as refining profits soar in reaction to Iran and Ukraine wars
